newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Belarus leader to sign union charter.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Belarus leader to sign union charter.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin and Belarus leader Alexander Lukashenko are due to sign a charter to govern a controversial union between their two Slav states on Friday amid uncertainty about its practical scope.

The Kremlin said in a statement on Thursday that Yeltsin and Lukashenko had finalised the text of the charter, aimed at filling in a largely declarative Union Treaty signed last month, at talks in Moscow.

Interfax news agency quoted Lukashenko as saying after the meeting that it took him and Yeltsin one hour to finalise the document. He added that a disputed clause proclaiming the aim of building a joint federative state had been removed.
The Kremlin, which has not mentioned such a clause, declined to give details of the meeting.
Lukashenko made clear before the start of the talks that Belarus would remain a sovereign state, rejecting a suggestion by Yeltsin that some kind of federation could be formed.
"We have a certain limit -- our Soviet experience. Under the Soviet Union we (Belarus) had our own United Nations membership," Lukashenko said before he left Minsk.
Yeltsin said earlier this week that he saw Russia and Belarus merging into a single federative state by the end of the integration process, comments which prompted an angry reaction in Minsk.
Belarus negotiators were seeking a tight union between two independent states, each of which would have equal rights.

Nationalist opponents of Lukashenko's hardline rule Belarus have condemned the planned union as a plot by Moscow to revive the empire and rob Minsk of the independence it won when the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
A few dozen demonstrators marched through Minsk on Thursday to protest against the planned union. They burned down a Russian flag and tore portraits of Lukashenko. Police did not interfere.
Russian liberals bitterly oppose the union, saying a deal with Belarus, where the transition from communism has been slow, could hurt Russian democracy and tarnish Russia's image abroad.
But opinion polls show that the majority of the population in both states support the idea of close integration between the two former Soviet republics.

A declarative Union Treaty was signed on April 2 after a last-minute intervention by newly-appointed liberals in the Russian government nervous that the original document gave Lukashenko too much power.
The charter, initialled at the same time, was then opened to public debate but details of what the final version involves have been kept under wraps.
On arriving in Moscow early on Thursday Lukashenko clearly toned down the importance of Friday's signing.
"I came to seal things 'de jure' the things which have already happened 'de facto,'" Itar-Tass news agency quoted him as saying.
